heading: Q1: Walk me through a P1 you handled end to end.
parentHeading: Scenario 1 --- Mount Point / P1 Batch Failure
content:
Sure. So this was during a night shift --- we suddenly started getting
around 17 alerts from Dynatrace, all saying batch jobs were failing.
Since it was hitting multiple jobs and clearly critical, I opened a P1
right away.

While I was opening the ticket, I logged into the Unix server in
parallel and started going through the logs. That's when I found the
actual cause --- the mount point where the process writes its logs had
filled up completely, 100%, and that's what was making every job on it
fail.

Since it was outside business hours, I started the bridge call
immediately and pulled in the on-call support team. I also sent out an
email to the distribution list letting everyone know a P1 was open,
listed the impacted jobs, and after checking with the team, gave a
2-hour ETA.

For the immediate fix, I worked with the Linux team to free up space on
that mount point. Once that was done, I reran the failed jobs one by one
--- had to be careful about the dependencies between them so I didn't
rerun something out of order. Everything came back clean after that.

Then, as a permanent fix, I got that mount point added as a monitoring
parameter in our alerting --- so now we get notified at 75% full instead
of waiting until it's completely full and jobs start failing. I closed
it out with an update email covering both the temporary and the
permanent fix.

heading: Q2: What's your process when a batch job fails at 2 AM?
parentHeading: Scenario 1 --- Mount Point / P1 Batch Failure
content:
First thing is I check the alert source --- Dynatrace or Splunk --- to
see how many jobs are actually affected and whether it's isolated or
part of a bigger pattern. If it's one job, I treat it as a regular
incident and start working the logs. But if it's multiple critical jobs
like in that mount point case, I open a P1 immediately rather than
waiting to investigate further first.

Once the P1's open, I start the bridge call and pull in whoever's
on-call --- I check our Confluence on-call page for that. While the
bridge is spinning up, I'm already in the Unix server pulling logs to
find the actual cause. I don't wait for the bridge to start
troubleshooting --- those happen in parallel.

Once I've identified the issue, I fix it, rerun the failed jobs
respecting their dependencies, and confirm everything's clean.
Throughout this, I'm sending hourly updates to the distribution list so
stakeholders know the status even if there's nothing new to report yet.

heading: Q3: How do you prevent the same issue from recurring?
parentHeading: Scenario 1 --- Mount Point / P1 Batch Failure
content:
That's really where the permanent fix comes in, separate from the
immediate fix. In the mount point case, increasing the space that night
got the jobs running again, but it didn't stop it from filling up again
next month.

So the permanent fix was adding that mount point as a threshold-based
alert --- 75% full --- so we get a heads-up before it becomes a P1 again
instead of after.

More broadly, if an incident like these repeats, it stops being treated
as just an incident and becomes a Problem. We do a proper root cause
analysis --- we follow the 5-why method --- and if it needs a code or
infra change, we raise a Jira ticket, tag all the related incidents to
it, and the fix goes through the normal SDLC and change management
process before it's closed out.

So it's not just about closing the ticket --- it's about making sure
I'm not doing the same 2 AM fix again three months later.

heading: Q1: Tell me about a time you found a data issue using SQL.
content:
This one wasn't reported to me --- I caught it myself while doing
routine data validation. I was running my usual SQL checks on the
transaction tables and noticed a mismatch --- some transaction records
didn't line up with what I'd expect based on the account data.

I dug into it and traced it back to a batch timing issue --- one batch
had run before another batch it actually depended on had finished.

So it processed against incomplete data. Once I confirmed that with a
few more targeted queries, I coordinated with the application team to do
a corrected re-run of the batch in the right order, then went back and
validated the data again with SQL to confirm everything was accurate.

I think this one's a good example of catching something proactively
instead of waiting for a customer to report it."

heading: Q2: How do you validate that production data is correct?
content:
I usually go table by table depending on what I'm checking. For
something like transaction data, I'll compare counts and sums between
the source and the downstream table, check for duplicates, and look at
timestamps to make sure batches ran in the right sequence.

I write queries using joins, group by, and sometimes window functions
like ROW_NUMBER if I'm checking for duplicate or out-of-order records.

If something looks off, I don't just fix it --- I first confirm whether
it's actually a data issue or just how the business logic is supposed
to work, because not every mismatch is a bug.

Once I've confirmed it's genuinely wrong, I trace it back --- was it a
job that failed, a dependency that didn't wait, a timing issue --- and
only then do I decide the fix, whether that's a manual correction or a
batch re-run.

heading: Q3: What's the difference between a symptom and a root cause?
content:
A symptom is what you actually see on the surface --- in this case, the
transaction data not matching.

A root cause is why it happened in the first place --- which here was
the batch timing dependency issue, one job running before its
predecessor had finished.

If I just fix the symptom --- manually correct that one mismatched
record --- it'll happen again next time the batches run in the wrong
order. Fixing the root cause means making sure the dependency is
actually enforced, so the second batch physically can't start until the
first one's done.

That's really the difference between an incident fix and a
problem-management fix --- one restores service, the other stops it from
happening again.

heading: Q1: Have you ever led a major incident bridge call? Walk me through it.
parentHeading: Scenario 3 --- Online Banking Login Outage / Bridge Call
content:
Yes --- online banking login went down, which is about as
customer-facing as it gets for a bank, so I opened it as a P1
immediately.

The first thing I did was start the bridge call. I pulled in the
application team first, since login failures usually point there, then
infrastructure right behind them in case it was server or network
related, and I looped in my manager as well since it was customer-facing
and leadership needed visibility.

If it had turned out to be a database issue I'd have pulled DBA in too,
but based on the initial symptoms, app and infra were the right first
call.

Once everyone was on, I coordinated between the teams while they worked
in parallel --- app team checking the service logs, infra checking
server health. I sent hourly status updates to the distribution list the
whole time, even when there wasn't a breakthrough yet, just to keep
everyone aligned on where we stood.

For the ETA, I didn't just guess --- I checked in with whichever team
had found the likely cause and asked for their honest estimate, then
communicated that, and adjusted it if things changed.

We got it restored within SLA, and after that I documented the full RCA
in Confluence --- what happened, what we did, and what we're doing to
stop it recurring.

heading: Q2: How do you communicate during a customer-facing outage?
parentHeading: Scenario 3 --- Online Banking Login Outage / Bridge Call
content:
Frequency and honesty, mainly. As soon as the P1 is opened, I send out
an initial notification to the distribution list so everyone knows
we're aware and working it --- I don't wait until I have the full
picture.

After that, I send updates every hour, even if the update is just
'still investigating with the app team, next update in an hour.'
That's better than silence, because silence makes people assume
nothing's happening.

I also make sure the updates have the actual impact --- which systems or
customers are affected --- not just technical details, because different
people on that distribution list need different things: leadership wants
business impact, the technical teams want the specifics.

Once it's resolved, I send a final closure update with a short summary
of what happened and what's being done to prevent it going forward.

heading: Q3: What goes into an RCA document?
parentHeading: Scenario 3 --- Online Banking Login Outage / Bridge Call
content:
I write it up in Confluence, and it typically covers: what the issue was
and its business impact, the timeline --- when it started, when we
noticed it, when it was resolved --- who was involved on the bridge,
what the immediate fix was to restore service, and then the actual root
cause once we've dug into it properly, usually using the 5-why
approach.

Then it covers the permanent fix --- what's being changed so this
doesn't happen again --- and if that needs code or infra changes, I
link the Jira ticket raised for it.

I keep it factual and structured so anyone on the team, even someone who
wasn't on the bridge call, can read it later and understand exactly
what happened and why.

heading: Q1: What is job dependency in Autosys, and how do you troubleshoot it?
parentHeading: Scenario 4 --- Autosys Dependency / Loan Interest Posting
content:
In Autosys, jobs often aren't standalone --- a job can be set to only
start once another job, its predecessor, has completed successfully.
That's a dependency. It's defined in the JIL, the Job Information
Language, when the job's set up.

When a job hasn't triggered and I suspect it's a dependency issue, I
run autorep -j on that job to check its current status, and I also check
the predecessor job's status.

If the predecessor is still running, failed, or stuck, that explains why
the dependent job never kicked off --- it's just waiting. Depending on
the situation, I'll either wait for the predecessor to finish
naturally, escalate if it's stuck, or if I've confirmed it's safe,
force the dependent job to run using sendevent.

I always double check dependencies before forcing anything, though,
because running things out of order on a banking batch can cause exactly
the kind of data mismatch I mentioned earlier.

heading: Q2: Tell me about a time a delayed job had a business impact.
parentHeading: Scenario 4 --- Autosys Dependency / Loan Interest Posting
content:
The end-of-day Autosys job for loan interest posting was delayed. When I
looked into it, I found it was a dependency issue --- a predecessor job
hadn't completed, so the interest posting job never got triggered in
the first place.

This one mattered because loan interest posting is time-sensitive ---
customers and internal systems expect that to run and reflect by end of
day, so a delay there isn't just a technical miss, it has a real
business and SLA impact if it isn't caught.

I identified the dependency failure, worked through it, and got the
schedule back on track within SLA.

It's a good example of why I don't just look at 'the job failed' ---
I look at why it's stuck, because with EOD banking jobs, timing itself
is part of the business requirement, not just a technical detail."

heading: Q1: How do you troubleshoot a file transfer failure?
parentHeading: Scenario 5 --- Recurring SFTP File Transfer Failure
content:
First, I check the transfer logs --- SFTP and WinSCP logs --- to see
exactly where it's failing: is it a connection issue, an authentication
issue, or is the file just not landing on the other end.

In our setup, SFTP was configured with passwordless authentication, so
if it's failing at the connection stage, that's usually a sign
something's off with the keys or the target server, not a typo'd
password.

For this particular recurring issue, I went through the logs over a few
occurrences instead of just looking at one failure in isolation, and
that's how I spotted the pattern --- it wasn't random, it was
happening under a specific condition. Once I understood the pattern,
instead of just fixing it that one time, I documented a proper
workaround in our KEDB so the next person hitting it doesn't have to
dig through logs from scratch --- they can just follow the steps.

heading: Q2: What's the difference between FTP, SFTP, and SCP?
parentHeading: Scenario 5 --- Recurring SFTP File Transfer Failure
content:
FTP is the plain File Transfer Protocol --- you connect, log in with a
username and password, and use commands like get and put to download or
upload files. It's not encrypted, so it's not something we'd use for
sensitive banking data.

SFTP is Secure FTP --- same idea, but encrypted, and in our project it
was set up with passwordless authentication using keys, so files could
move securely without typing a password every time.

SCP, Secure Copy, is a bit different --- it's meant for a quick
point-to-point copy between machines over a secure connection. It
doesn't open an interactive session like FTP does --- it just transfers
the file and exits. If passwordless auth isn't set up, it'll prompt
for a password. So depending on the situation --- interactive session
versus a one-shot secure copy --- we'd pick FTP, SFTP, or SCP.

heading: Q3: What goes into a KEDB workaround entry vs a permanent fix?
parentHeading: Scenario 5 --- Recurring SFTP File Transfer Failure
content:
A workaround entry is about restoring service fast --- it documents the
steps to get around the issue right now, without necessarily fixing
what's causing it underneath.

For the SFTP case, that meant writing down exactly what to check in the
logs and what steps got the transfer going again, so the next engineer
isn't starting from zero at 2 AM.

A permanent fix is different --- that's addressing the actual root
cause so the issue stops happening altogether. That usually means it's
gone through problem management --- a proper RCA, a Jira ticket for
whatever needs to change, and it goes through SDLC and change management
before it's deployed.

Once the permanent fix is live, I'd go back and update the KEDB entry
to reflect that, so it's clear there's now a real fix and not just a
workaround.

heading: Q1: Tell me about a time you caught an issue after a deployment.
content:
During a core banking release --- this would've gone through our normal
change window --- I was doing the standard post-deployment health check
afterward, and I noticed something that didn't look right. It wasn't a
full outage or anything customers were reporting yet, but it was enough
of an anomaly that I didn't want to just note it and move on.

I escalated it right away instead of waiting to see if it got worse.
That turned out to be the right call --- the team was able to look into
it and fix it before it actually impacted any business SLA or customer.

If I'd waited, it could easily have turned into a full incident instead
of something we caught early.

heading: Q2: What's your process for validating a release?
content:
After a change is deployed --- usually during our Friday night to
Saturday morning change window --- my job as production support is to do
a health check on the application.

We have a checklist for this: confirming the app is up, the key portals
and functionalities are working, and I go through it manually rather
than assuming it's fine just because the deployment itself succeeded.

I'm specifically looking for anything that doesn't match expected
behavior --- error rates, functionality that looks off, anything unusual
in the logs right after deployment.

If everything checks out, I sign off. If something looks even slightly
off, I don't wait for it to escalate on its own --- I raise it.

heading: Q3: Have you ever had to escalate something that wasn't yet a full incident?
content:
Yes --- that post-deployment anomaly is a good example. At the point I
noticed it, it hadn't caused a customer-facing incident yet, so
technically I could've just kept monitoring it.

But the way I think about it: if something's deviating from expected
behaviour right after a change went into production, and there's a real
chance it could grow into something bigger or hit an SLA, it's better
to flag it early and let the right people make the call, rather than sit
on it and hope it resolves itself.

At the same time, I try not to escalate every small blip --- that just
creates noise and makes people stop taking escalations seriously.

So the judgment call is really about impact and trend: is this something
that's isolated and likely to stay that way, or something that's tied
to a change we just made and could scale up. In this case it was clearly
the latter, so I flagged it immediately, and it got fixed before it
became a real incident.
